topic: diagnosing a laid hedgerow that has gone gappy along a field boundary

provenance.author: glowny-en-e
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is a closed arithmetic tally of a hedging order (stretches, stakes, binders, bundles, hours) with one closed task question per turn, base is a diagnosis of thin regrowth after laying. Grounded external referent: the old earth bank the stools sit on, named in turn 0 and again immediately before every insertion, and it remains the leading suspect throughout.

a: Work through the hedge order for the top field, taking the four stretches one by one.
Stretch one runs sixty metres and stretch two runs forty-five metres along the same boundary.
Stretch three runs twenty-four metres, while stretch four runs fifteen metres up to the gate.
Set the stretches out from longest to shortest, and state the length reached after each one.
How many metres does the whole boundary come to once the four have been added?
base: We laid the hedge along the top field two winters ago and it has gone gappy already.
The stools sit on an old bank that runs the whole length of the boundary.
The bank is dry and crumbling at the north end, where most of the gaps are.
We cut and laid in late March, right after the frosts had finally let go.
Where would you start looking for the reason the regrowth came so thin?

a: Set out longest first, the order runs stretch one, stretch two, stretch three, stretch four.
The lengths reached after each one are sixty, then one hundred five, then one hundred twenty-nine metres.
The last figure comes to one hundred forty-four metres for the whole boundary.
At one stake to the metre that comes to one hundred forty-four stakes in all.
Does the figure of one hundred forty-four metres match the length on the survey sheet?
base: The bank is where I would start, because a dry crest starves the stools of water.
A pleacher needs sap moving through the hinge, and a thirsty stool will not push.
Late March is also very late, since the sap is up and the cuts bleed.
I would want to know how deep the soil sits on the bank at that north end.
Do the stools at the wet end of the bank carry more growth than the dry ones?

a: Now work out the binders, at one binder for every three metres of laid hedge.
Give the binder count for all four stretches in the order you set them out.
Whips go in at four to the metre wherever a gap runs longer than two metres.
Put stretches one and two on the first day, and the other two on the second.
Which binder count belongs to stretch three at that fixed rate per metre?
base: The soil on the bank is barely a spade deep before you hit stone and rubble.
The wet end carries far more growth, and the stools there have thrown up strong shoots.
We drove stakes every metre and bound the tops with hazel from the same hedge.
The sheep lean on the thin stretch and there is a smooth run where they push through.
Would filling the gaps with new whips be enough on its own?

a: Stretch one takes twenty binders and stretch two takes fifteen binders at that same rate.
Stretch three takes eight binders, and stretch four takes five binders on the run to the gate.
The first day therefore needs thirty-five binders and one hundred five stakes in all.
The second day needs thirteen binders and thirty-nine stakes for the two shorter stretches.
Does the binder total of forty-eight agree with the count written in the store book?
base: New whips alone will struggle, because the same thin soil will hold them back too.
I would build the bank back up first with turf and spoil from the ditch below.
Then plant the gaps in winter and guard them, since the sheep will find them fast.
Stakes at one metre are fine, but the binding wants renewing every few years.
How much spoil could you lift out of that ditch without cutting into the roots?

a: One correction before we go on: stretch three runs thirty metres and not twenty-four.
Redo its binders and its stakes, and leave the other three stretches exactly as they are.
Then give the new totals for length and for binders across the whole boundary.
After that list the four stretches in the order the crew will work them.
Which stretch comes first under the order stretch two, stretch four, stretch one, stretch three?
base: The ditch is full of silt and we could take a good foot off the bottom.
That spoil would go straight onto the bank if the digger can reach along the headland.
Nobody has touched that bank in thirty years, and the ditch has never been dug out.
The old boys used to trim the hedge every second winter with a hook.
Could a proper trim bring the thin stretch back without laying it all again?

a: Stretch three at thirty metres now takes ten binders and thirty stakes of its own.
The new length total is one hundred fifty metres along the whole field boundary.
The new binder total comes to fifty across the four stretches taken all together.
The stake count rises to one hundred fifty at one stake to the metre.
Does the working order still open with stretch two exactly as it was set out?
base: A trim will thicken what is there, but it cannot make a stool throw new stems.
Where the gaps run to a metre or more, you need planting rather than trimming.
I would lay the thin stretch again in November, once the leaves are off.
Cut low, keep the hinge wide and lean every pleacher the same way up the slope.
Do you have hazel of your own for the stakes and binders this winter?

a: Turn the whole stake order into bundles, at forty stakes to the bundle.
Tell me how many full bundles that needs and how many stakes are left over.
Then split the binder total between two loads of equal size, and give each figure.
The crew starts at eight in the morning and lays fifteen metres every hour.
How many full bundles does a count of one hundred fifty stakes come to?
base: There is a hazel coppice in the far corner and it has not been cut for years.
We could get stakes and binders out of it if we start early in the autumn.
The bank at the north end still worries me, since the spoil will take a season to settle.
Laying into loose spoil sounds like a way to lose half the stools again.
Should the rebuilding wait a full year before we lay that stretch?

a: One hundred fifty stakes make three full bundles with thirty stakes left standing over.
Each of the two loads of binders holds twenty-five binders for the work.
At fifteen metres an hour stretch one takes four hours from the eight o'clock start.
Stretch two takes three hours, and stretch three takes two hours on the second day.
Stretch four takes one hour, closing a run of ten hours across the two days.
base: Let the spoil settle one winter, then lay the stretch the following November.
Plant the worst gaps this year so the whips have two seasons before the laying.
Guard each whip with a spiral and keep the sheep off that side until spring.
Cut the hazel in the same autumn so the stakes go in green and drive well.
Mark the stools you plant so the notes tell you which ones took and which failed.

a: Print a short list of the four steps in order for the crew tomorrow morning.
Step one is cutting the stems, step two is laying them and step three is staking.
Step four is binding, and each step needs the clock time for stretch one.
Cutting starts at eight in the morning and the binding finishes at twelve exactly.
Which clock time closes the laying if cutting and laying take one hour each?
base: That gives us a clear order, and the hazel cut fits neatly into the same autumn.
I will mark the new whips with tags so nobody trims them by mistake next summer.
One worry is the far end, where the ditch runs wet and the ground stays soft.
If the digger works there in winter it will churn the headland into a mess.
Should the ditch work wait for a dry spell in late summer instead?

a: Step one is the cutting at eight, and it runs a full hour on stretch one.
Step two is the laying from nine until ten, exactly as you set it out.
Step three is the staking between ten and eleven along the same stretch.
Step four is the binding from eleven until twelve, which closes stretch one.
Stretch two follows at twelve, and that order holds through the rest of the day.
base: Yes, take the ditch out in August when the ground carries a machine without damage.
The spoil dries on the bank through the autumn and settles before the frosts.
Then the planting goes in during December, straight into ground that has firmed up.
The laying follows a winter later, with your own stakes and binders ready to hand.
Two seasons of that and the thin stretch will be as tight as the rest.
